title: Why this matters
text: Before a buyer can work with a new supplier, someone needs to know whether the business details and supporting proof describe the same entity. When they do not, the supplier and reviewer both need a clear next step. This demo follows that decision from submission through resolution.

title: A clean submission runs
text: Here is Apex Components, a fictional practice supplier. The demo fill uses only details linked to this account; the vendor still reviews the business information, required documents and legal declarations before submitting. Watch the document reading and validation stages run after the click. The application reference and processing result are then saved. A supplier can return to see what happened, while the buyer can inspect the evidence behind the outcome. The form is an entry point into a real review workflow, rather than a decorative success screen.

title: Procurement sets ownership
text: The procurement desk sees the new application alongside the rest of its organisation's queue. Each case shows its status, priority and next action, so staff can quickly work out what needs attention. Procurement assigns Rajesh Iyer as the reviewer. That creates an accountable handoff and makes the case visible in his review desk. Procurement coordinates the work, while the final approval is reserved for a reviewer.

title: Human decision and evidence
text: Rajesh opens a case assigned to him. The case brings the submitted business details, uploaded proof, automated findings and decision controls together. He can trace why a check passed or failed before making a judgment. A green check is useful preparation; it is not an autonomous approval. For this clean supplier, the documents and declared details are consistent. Rajesh records an approval with a reason, and the decision becomes part of the activity trail. The same controls would block approval while a serious issue remains open.

title: The supplier hears back
text: The vendor sees the approval on its own dashboard and receives an in-app notice that opens the decision receipt. The receipt includes the application reference and decision date, and says there are no remaining application tasks. That closes the loop for the supplier instead of leaving them staring at a submitted status. Approval here means the onboarding review is complete; it does not claim to activate purchasing access or payments.

title: A subtle conflict runs
text: Now watch a second prepared draft being submitted live. It sits in a separate fictional buyer workspace, so there is no unrelated duplicate supplier signal. The company PAN looks plausible. The GST number also looks plausible at a glance. But a GST number contains the taxpayer PAN, and this one embeds a different company's PAN. The draft has no validation result before this submission. When the vendor clicks Submit, Zamp runs the checks, saves the failed cross-field finding and holds approval. The case tells the vendor to confirm which entity's credentials were supplied. This is more useful than rejecting a field just because its format looks wrong: both fields have the right shape, yet together they tell a contradictory story. A reviewer can see the issue and the evidence without hunting through a technical log.

title: Correction remains a review
text: The vendor can respond in the same place as the request. Here they enter the GST number that matches the declared company PAN and explain the correction. A new check runs against the revised value. The reviewer queue then marks the case as having a supplier reply, and the response is visible inside the case. The previous failed run stays in history, so the change can be understood later. This reply does not silently turn into an approval: the assigned reviewer must assess the new evidence and record the decision.

title: History and honest uncertainty
text: Processing Runs keeps the conflict result and the check that produced it. A separate prepared case shows a registry timeout. That is unknown evidence, rather than proof the vendor is wrong, so staff should retry or review it. The supplier is not asked to repair a registry outage. Every document and registry response in this recording is synthetic. In a pilot, I would measure decision time, unsafe approvals, and valid suppliers held unnecessarily. The goal is a faster, clearer decision with a defensible record.
